BUSINESS_CONFIDENCE.label: Business expectations and confidence as an influence on investment

stages.name: Animal spirits
stages.title: Animal spirits
stages.sub: Why waves of optimism and pessimism, not just cold calculation, drive investment decisions.

steps.q: A firm is deciding whether to build a new factory. It tries to work out how much profit the factory will make over the next ten years. Can it know this for certain?
steps.wrong: Yes, if it does the sums carefully
steps.hint: Ten years of future sales and costs: is that something you can calculate exactly, or only estimate?

steps.q: Nobody knows exactly what interest rates, prices or government policy will be in five years' time. Does that make the firm's guess about future profit more or less reliable?
steps.hint: If the future itself is unclear, can any estimate of it be solid?

steps.q: Faced with that uncertainty, two firms with identical numbers on paper choose differently, one builds the factory, one doesn't. What must be driving the difference?
steps.right: How they feel about the future, not just the figures
steps.wrong: One of them made an arithmetic mistake
steps.hint: The numbers are the same for both. So what else could explain the different choice?
steps.pre: So beyond the figures, firms are swayed by

steps.q: Business confidence surges and firms across the whole economy suddenly start investing more, even though nothing in their actual sales figures has changed yet. What is really driving this wave of extra investment?
steps.right: A shared mood of optimism spreading between firms
steps.wrong: A rise in firms' actual measured profits
steps.hint: It's the name Keynes gave to gut feeling and mood, not to the measurable data.
steps.pre: Keynes called this wave of feeling
